newsitem.title: USA: Key West says farewell to Hemingway fiesta.
newsitem.headline: Key West says farewell to Hemingway fiesta.

text.p: The bell has tolled for Key West's Hemingway Days festival, a boozy celebration of the writer's life held every July in the Florida Keys island where he lived and wrote for a decade.
Ernest Hemingway's sons said the festivities had become so commercialized that they were no longer a suitable tribute to the Nobel Laureate, son Patrick Hemingway said on Wednesday.
Rather than slug it out in court, Key West organisers said they would simply cancel the fiesta.

That means no Hemingway look-alike contest, no tour of Hemingway's favourite haunts such as Sloppy Joe's Bar on Duvall Street and Captain Tony's Saloon round the corner, and no short story competition for aspiring writers.
The festival, held since 1981, draws about 10,000 people to Key West, many of them sporting white beards and hefty paunches and bidding to outdo each other in bravado and boozing.

"We think it is very lacking in taste. We think it is a travesty on the memory of Ernest Hemingway," Patrick said by phone from his home in Bozeman, Montana. "We think it has gone on long enough. We believe it is no longer tolerable."
The family also planned its own event to mark the centennial in 1999 of his birth, he said.

Hemingway lived in Key West from 1929 to 1940, fishing, drinking and writing such works as "Death in the Afternoon" and "The Snows of Kilimanjaro." The novel "To Have and Have Not" is set in Key West, and he reputedly met his third wife, Martha Gelhorn at the bar in Sloppy Joe's.
His house and other Hemingway landmarks draw crowds of tourists each year.

"To lose the festival is to lose some of that identity that has shaped Key West. That's the real loss, not the marketing loss," said Hemingway scholar James Plath of Illinois Wesleyan University in Bloomington.

The trouble over who would have and have not control of the 10-day event began in February when Marla Metzner, a New York-based licensing represtentative for the Hemingway sons, sent a letter to festival organiser Michael Walton.
The letter, seen by Reuters, demanded control, a 10 per cent cut of proceeds, and back payments from the previous five years. It implied a law suit if organisers did not comply.
Walton said lawyers advised him it would be costly to fight and the winner would not take all. "The town would be dragged through the mud," he said.
Lorian Hemingway, Ernest's grand-daughter and Gregory's daughter, lashed out at her relatives' actions. She is a judge of the short-story contest.
"How can people who use the Hemingway name to sell shot guns call this festival crass?" she said from her home in Seattle.
She was refering to a controversy several years ago when Patrick licensed the family name to sell a brand of shotgun. Ernest Hemingway shot himself dead with a shotgun in 1961.

Patrick told Reuters: "There's no defence to that. All I can say it is no longer the case." He said the family was protecting its rights and if it had made mistakes in taste and judgment that was its own affair.
Another old acquaintance of Hemingway's, Cuban President Fidel Castro, is also hoping to benefit from the enduring fascination with the writer.

Cuban tour operators in Mexico on Tuesday launched the forthcoming 47th edition of the Ernest Hemingway International Billfish Fishing Tournament as part of a drive to diversify the island's increasingly vital tourist trade.
"The tournament is an important link with its founder, a great man who loved Cuba," said Marina Menocal, marketing director at the Hemingway Marina on the outskirts of Havana.
Hemingway lived in Cuba for 22 years after leaving Key West.
